implementation_notes: The modern C++ realization is the header-only jwt-cpp library: the builder chain is the claim assembler (set_issuer, set_subject, set_audience, set_key_id for the kid, set_issued_now, set_expires_in), and .sign(jwt::algorithm::rs256{public_key, private_key, ...}) is the signing authority, returning the compact assertion as a std::string; jwt::verify() with allow_algorithm is the consumer mirror. What replaces the classic structure: the library supplies the JSON handling (any JSON library via traits), the base64 variants and the crypto via OpenSSL, LibreSSL or wolfSSL, so your code keeps only the policy wrapper - a fixed issuer, a mandatory claim set and the key lookup. The classic hand-rolled builder remains justified only when the project must emit SAML XML instead of JWS.
pitfalls: Constructing jwt::algorithm::rs256 re-parses the PEM keys; build it once per key and reuse it, because key parsing dominates issuance cost.
Being header-only means the library is compiled with your flags: check its documented build knobs (JWT_DISABLE_BASE64, exception/RTTI settings) before blaming the crypto.
A token signed with a key nobody can fetch is unverifiable: publishing the matching JWK/JWKS is a separate step that jwt-cpp does not perform for you.
Set the key id before signing - adding a kid to the header afterwards changes the signing input and invalidates the signature.

variants.name: Hand-built compact JWS over OpenSSL EVP (no token library)
variants.implementation_notes: The dependency-light route for toolchains that predate C++11 or forbid a header-only dependency: serialize header and claim set with whatever JSON writer the project already links, base64url-encode both segments, sign the ASCII signing input with EVP_DigestSign over an EVP_PKEY and concatenate the encoded signature. Choose it only with a reason, because you then own every detail - alphabet and padding, claim serialization, algorithm allowlist and key-size policy - that a JOSE library would have owned, and RFC 8725's guidance about implementation quality applies in full. JWS has one advantage over XML-DSig here: the encoded segments are signed verbatim, so no canonicalisation step can silently change the signing input.
pitfalls: The two-call EVP_DigestSign length query is mandatory; a guessed buffer size corrupts memory or truncates the signature.
base64url is not base64: URL-safe alphabet, no padding, and no newlines - OpenSSL's BIO base64 encoder inserts line breaks unless told otherwise.
The signature covers exactly the segments you send, so re-encoding the payload after signing (different whitespace or key order) breaks verification with a confusing 'invalid signature'.
No library means no algorithm allowlist: your own code must reject alg values it was not compiled to produce, including none.
